::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[What do the three dots mean in this problem? (Concrete Mathematics, ex. 1.9)](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4774742/what-do-the-three-dots-mean-in-this-problem-concrete-mathematics-ex-1-9), asked by [Noah J](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1086124/noah-j) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-09-24; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Exercise 1.9 in Concrete Mathematics (Knuth et al.):
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: rYmyr.png
>
> What does '...' between $x_1$ and $x_n$ mean? If it's multiplication, I would expect the dots to be centered. If it's saying that the inequality holds for each $x_a$ with a between $1$ and $n$ (inclusive), then I would expect commas.
:::

Yes, it denotes multiplication. As I wrote in my comment three years ago, the part after “This is true when $n=2$, since...” has $x_1x_2$ multiplied. And the statement to be proven in the exercise is the [AM-GM inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AM%E2%80%93GM_inequality), which has a product.

I did some exploration with the [fonts](https://ctan.org/pkg/concmath), and Misha Lavrov looked into the [TeX macros](https://ctan.org/pkg/gkpmac) used to typeset the book. It appears that the authors indeed intended an ellipsis along the baseline (`\ldots`), even though we now normally write it above the baseline (`\cdots`) in these contexts.
